function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a complete “starter kit” you can drop into the **nodejs‑welcome** repository.  
It contains:

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `Dockerfile` | Builds a lightweight Node JS image |
| `k8s/deployment.yaml` + `k8s/service.yaml` | Deploys the app to a Kubernetes cluster |
| `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | CI pipeline that builds, tests, pushes the image and (optionally) deploys it |

> **NOTE** – The repo you mentioned is a Node.js project, so the Docker image must be based on a Node base image.  
> The helper functions you saw only support Python images, so we’ll hand‑craft the Dockerfile instead.

---

## 1. Clone the repo

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> If you already have the repo locally, just `cd` into it.

---

## 2. Create the required files

### 2.1 Dockerfile

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
# ------------------------------------
# Use the official Node.js 18 slim image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Create app directory
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package files first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install production dependencies
RUN npm install --production

# Copy the rest of the source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port your app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> *If your app listens on a different port, change `EXPOSE 3000` and the `CMD` accordingly.*

---

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAMLs

Create a folder `k8s` and add two files inside it.

#### `k8s/deployment.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: <YOUR_DOCKER_REGISTRY>/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- replace
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
```

#### `k8s/service.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> Replace `<YOUR_DOCKER_REGISTRY>` with the registry you’ll push to (e.g. `docker.io/zelarhq`).

---

### 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow

Create the directory `.github/workflows` and add `ci.yml`.

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout code
      uses: actions/checkout@v3

    - name: Set up Node.js
      uses: actions/setup-node@v3
      with:
        node-version: '18'

    - name: Install dependencies
      run: npm ci

    - name: Run tests
      run: npm test

    - name: Build Docker image
      run: |
        docker build -t ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} .
        echo ${{ secrets.DOCKER_PASSWORD }} | docker login -u ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }} --password-stdin
        docker push ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}

    - name: Deploy to Kubernetes (optional)
      uses: azure/k8s-deploy@v1
      with:
        manifests: |
          ./k8s/deployment.yaml
          ./k8s/service.yaml
        images: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}
        kubeconfig: ${{ secrets.KUBECONFIG }}
```

> **Secrets you’ll need to set in the repo settings**  
> * `DOCKER_USERNAME` – your Docker Hub (or other registry) username  
> * `DOCKER_PASSWORD` – password or personal access token  
> * `KUBECONFIG` – base64‑encoded kubeconfig if you want automatic deployment

---

## 3. Add the new files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/*.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

---

## 4. Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

Once pushed, GitHub Actions will automatically run the workflow on every push to `main`.  
If you’re using a different branch strategy, adjust the `on.push.branches` section of the workflow accordingly.

---

### Quick sanity check

After the first push, you should see:

* A new **Actions** tab with a successful run.  
* In Docker Hub (or your registry), an image tagged with the commit SHA.  
* If you have a cluster configured, the deployment and service should appear in `kubectl get all`.

That’s it! Your repo now has a fully‑functional Docker build, Kubernetes deployment, and CI pipeline. Happy coding!
